name: Lena Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We’re independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government, and we don’t sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and run the eleven-person replenishment team for a large clothing retailer. A container arrives late, six stores ask for the same winter coats, and I have to decide which shelves go bare without pretending the stock exists. I like the moment a store manager says we got the right boxes there. I dislike the meeting in which someone calls a missed delivery a dashboard colour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you here, and what is life like outside the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have an MBA and know our supplier lead times better than anyone in the region, but the company froze my pay band after a takeover. I stayed because there are few comparable jobs near our mortgage, and my husband Martin teaches music lessons around our children’s school hours. Our daughter Ada is 16, our son Ben is seven, and the replacement boiler used up our savings last spring; we have about two weeks of bills in cash. I use AI now and then to draft a store update, but I let a colleague prove a tool before it touches an order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the stores that a better draft still needs a person to check the count on the loading sheet. If a coat never left the depot, a cheerful message will not put it on a rail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work would carry on, which ought to be reassuring. Yet the frozen pay band and two weeks in cash leave me watching every boiler noise like another bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I’d take the missed-delivery log to my line manager and ask for a pay-band review tied to the late shipments we fixed. In the first year I’d keep the loading-sheet signoff and postpone replacing our old sofa until we have a month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about money, even with the job still there. The boiler bill taught me how quickly a respectable salary can disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager see in that log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The store names, the promised dates and which boxes actually reached them. I want an answer about my pay, not a compliment for being indispensable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the sofa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The springs are going, but we can sit on it. A new sofa cannot pay a mortgage instalment when a music lesson cancels.

say: I’d keep a **loading-sheet check** before telling stores their coats are on the way.
I’d show managers **actual delivery dates** instead of treating a dashboard colour as proof.
think: My **job continues** if AI adds little to the work.
Our **frozen pay** and two-week cash reserve make another home repair frightening.
do: Request a **pay-band review** using the missed-delivery log next week.
Keep **loading-sheet signoff** and postpone a new sofa until one month of bills is saved.
feel: I feel **anxious** about money despite steady work.
S0.quote: A new sofa cannot pay a mortgage instalment when a music lesson cancels.
fieldNote: Her expertise keeps her employed despite a **low pay band** since the takeover.
The **boiler replacement** explains why her cash reserve is thin.
She asks for **documented pay recognition** before a plateau changes the job.

steps.text: Request pay-band review using the missed-delivery log next week
Postpone replacing the sofa until the household holds one month of bills in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the stores that AI can forecast demand and draft transfer orders, but no software should send an empty truck with a full delivery notice. The person loading the boxes should sign what actually went on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planners spend most of the day comparing orders and writing allocations, so a few could go without anyone touching a robot. My MBA and good record would not protect the manager of a team that has halved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I’d propose a four-week trial on the low-volume coat route, with the loader and two store managers signing the delivered counts each day. If those records match, I’d use the forecasting tool for that route in the first year, but ask the director to keep the signed paper trail and tell staff about any vacancy freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the planners and my own post. Trying one route gives us evidence. A successful coat-route AI trial could threaten planning jobs, including mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pick the quiet route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mistake there can be recovered without leaving a busy store empty for a weekend. The loader still has to be paid for the extra check; I will not hide testing in their lunch break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the forecasts are right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say so. I would also ask whose wages the company thinks it saves and whether the stores can still call a person when the truck is wrong.

say: I’d test AI on **one quiet route** while loaders and stores sign delivered counts.
Stores need a **human contact** when a truck arrives with the wrong boxes.
think: Much of our **planning work** could shrink before robots touch the depot.
My MBA cannot protect **my manager post** if the planning team is halved.
do: Propose a **four-week route trial** with paid loader checks and signed store counts.
Use the **forecast tool** only if counts match, and seek notice of any vacancy freeze.
feel: I feel **anxious** because success could mean fewer planners.
S1.quote: A successful coat-route AI trial could threaten planning jobs, including mine.
fieldNote: She will try AI **route by route** after colleagues verify deliveries.
She names her **own manager post** among possible losses.
The loader’s **paid checking time** is part of her trial condition.

steps.text: Propose a four-week forecast trial on one quiet route with paid loader and store checks
Use forecast tool only after signed truck and store counts match

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell store staff to keep the signed delivery sheets, because a wrong allocation still leaves customers staring at an empty rail. I’d ask the company for notice and a named person to answer stock disputes after any reorganisation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could do my allocation judgments and supplier calls better and cheaper; I expect the planning desk to close. Martin’s lessons rely on families paying, so I cannot assume his earnings will carry the mortgage, and hands-on loading only gets until about 2031 before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d ask the lender what temporary payment arrangements actually exist, without counting on approval, and put our second car up for sale only after checking that Martin can reach his pupils by bus and I can collect Ben; selling it would also end the second insurance and fuel bills. I’d also take small paid clothing repairs from neighbours only after they agree a price; in the first year after AGI arrives I’d keep any paid retailer shifts and use the car proceeds for the mortgage, rather than pretend repairs replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. Two weeks of cash is almost no runway if a planning department disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you really sell the car with two children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless Martin’s lesson journeys work by bus and I can still collect Ben from school. The car is worth money, but losing the lessons to save it would be foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who taught you clothing repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother showed me how to alter school uniforms, and I still do Ada’s hems. Three neighbours paying for uniform repairs would be a business; three neighbours complimenting a hem would not.

say: I’d tell stores to keep **signed delivery sheets** when an automated allocation is disputed.
The retailer should name a **human stock contact** and give staff written notice of reorganisation.
think: I expect my **planning desk to close** when 2028 AGI can make supplier and allocation decisions.
Martin’s **lesson income** cannot be assumed to carry the mortgage through a job loss.
do: Ask the **mortgage lender** about temporary terms without assuming approval.
Sell the **second car** only if lessons and school pickup work; take neighbour repairs at agreed prices.
Keep **paid retailer shifts** after 2028 and use any car proceeds for mortgage bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by two weeks of cash and expected job loss.
S2.quote: Three neighbours paying for uniform repairs would be a business; three neighbours complimenting a hem would not.
fieldNote: Her **thinking-heavy lead role** faces 2028 AGI directly.
A car sale depends on **bus access** and school pickup, not just resale value.
Paid uniform repairs are an **uncertain supplement**, not a replacement management wage.
Depot loading also faces **2031 robots** after planning work changes.

steps.text: Ask mortgage lender about temporary payment arrangements before 2028
Sell second car to end insurance and fuel bills only if lessons and Ben’s pickup work
Take small paid clothing repairs from neighbours only after agreeing a price
Keep paid retailer shifts after 2028 and direct car proceeds to mortgage bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company to show each planner which tasks are moving and the date, while there is still time to change the roster fairly. I would not promise a depot job is safe when the machines arrive later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives Ada time to finish school and us some chance to rebuild cash, if the frozen wage does not fall further. A depot shift might be paid for a while, but its paperwork faces 2031 AGI and its loading work faces robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 I’d set aside 35 each payday only when the mortgage and Martin’s lesson costs are paid, and keep asking for a pay-band correction each annual review. Before 2031 I’d apply for an advertised depot shift only if its written hours and wage cover my mortgage share and Ben’s pickup; in the first year after AGI I’d take that paid shift if offered, while checking how long the depot still needs human loaders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years lets me compare real rosters rather than guess from a course brochure. I would miss leading the planners, even if the title proves useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already took a lower pay band to stay near the children’s school. A title cannot make up the missing mortgage money. I would take a real paid shift if the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the depot will not offer you a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep applying for paid work and keep the savings untouched for bills. I would not quit my current job on the strength of a manager saying they might need help later.

say: I’d demand **task dates and rosters** while planners still have time to respond.
I would not sell a **depot shift** as permanent shelter from later machines.
think: Ada can finish school before **2031 AGI**; cash rebuilding depends on our pay holding.
The depot’s **paperwork faces AGI** before 2034 robots reach the loading work.
do: Set aside **35 each payday** only after mortgage and lesson costs are covered.
Apply for a **posted depot shift** only if written pay, hours and Ben’s pickup work.
Take **paid loading shifts** after 2031 only if offered and still staffed by people.
feel: I feel **anxious** but have time to compare real rosters.
S3.quote: A title cannot make up the missing mortgage money.
fieldNote: Her longer runway allows **small conditional savings**, without assuming a pay rise.
The depot vacancy needs **written hours and wage** plus school pickup.
She knows loading is a **short bridge** before 2034 robots.

steps.text: Save 35 each payday only after mortgage and lesson costs are paid
Apply before 2031 for posted depot shifts with written mortgage-share wages and workable pickup
Take paid depot loading shift after 2031 only if offered and people are still staffed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade is long enough to publish honest staffing plans and let people choose instead of waiting for a final letter. I would tell other parents that apprenticeships need real pay and an employer, not a glossy course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036; Ada will be 26 and Ben 17, so the school-run question changes but the mortgage may not be gone. Supplier planning and even depot scheduling face 2036 AGI, and physical loading follows robots around 2039; I cannot hide in a better title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From next summer I’d take paid alteration orders at the community market twice a month only if the first neighbours actually pay and Martin can cover Ben’s Saturday care. I’d keep the retailer salary while it lasts and put those repair earnings into cash savings; by 2036 I’d grow the work only if repeat orders pay more than materials and travel, and in the first year after AGI I’d continue it only while customers pay for human repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about being 53 and relying on tiny orders, but a decade would let me see demand before risking our mortgage. The repair table is something I can start without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rent a shop if the repairs grew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a hope. I would need steady paid orders after costs and enough cash for the mortgage before taking on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ben in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 17 he can choose an apprenticeship if a real employer pays him. I would not spend our housing money buying him a certificate with no paid place.

say: I’d ask the retailer for **honest staffing plans** while workers still have time to choose.
I’d tell parents an apprenticeship needs a **paying employer**, not just a course advert.
think: At 53 my **planning expertise** still faces 2036 AGI.
Ben will be **17**, and even depot loading faces 2039 robots after its scheduling changes.
do: Take **paid market repairs** twice monthly only after neighbours pay and Saturday care works.
Keep the **retailer salary** while available and save repair earnings after costs.
Grow **repairs** only on profitable repeat orders; rent only with steady net orders and mortgage cash; continue while customers pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to test demand slowly.
S4.quote: The repair table is something I can start without borrowing.
fieldNote: Her own **alteration skill** offers a small paid route with no course debt.
She tests **customer demand** before growing repairs or risking housing money.
The children are **26 and 17** by 2036, changing care needs.
Human repairs face **2039 robots** after planning work faces AGI.

steps.text: Take twice-monthly paid market alterations only after neighbours pay and Martin covers Saturday care
Save alteration earnings after materials and travel while retailer salary continues
Grow repairs on profitable repeat orders; rent only with steady net orders and mortgage cash
Continue human repairs after 2036 only while customers pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Our boiler swallowed the reserve, and I expect allocation work to go before I can build another one. A real notice date, clear mortgage options and paid shifts I can actually reach would help more than another compliment about my MBA.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would miss the work. I would miss telling a store manager the coats really were on the truck, with my own name behind the answer. An empty rail is not a colour on a dashboard.

headlineQuote: An empty rail is not a colour on a dashboard.
portrait: **Lena**, 43, leads eleven planners for a large clothing retailer and knows supplier lead times intimately.
A frozen **low pay band** and boiler replacement leave her with two weeks of bills in cash.
Her husband’s **music lessons** vary, while Ada is 16 and Ben is seven.
She tests **one AI route**, considers paid depot shifts, and checks whether neighbours buy clothing repairs.
The **2028 deadline** frightens her most because planning work may vanish before cash recovers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close her allocation desk while the household has only two weeks of cash.
whatWouldHelp: A **real notice date**, clear mortgage options and reachable paid shifts would help her plan.
